html:
The Cape Colony was a Dutch and then British colony at the southern tip of Africa, from 1652 to 1910, the core of what became South Africa. The map shows it from 1715 to 1900.

The Dutch East India Company settled the Cape in 1652 as a supply station for ships to Asia. Company servants became free farmers. The colony depended on slaves brought from Asia, Madagascar and Mozambique.

As settlers spread inland as cattle farmers, called trekboers, they took the land and herds of the Khoisan. In the east, from 1779, the colony fought a century of frontier wars with the Xhosa.

British rule:

  • Britain took the Cape in 1795, gave it back in 1803, and seized it for good in 1806.
  • Slavery ended in 1834. Many Dutch-speaking farmers, resenting British rule, left on the Great Trek and founded republics to the north.
  • The diamond rush at Kimberley from 1871 brought wealth and made Cecil Rhodes, prime minister from 1890 to 1896.

After the Boer War, the Cape joined Natal, the Transvaal and the Orange River Colony in the Union of South Africa in 1910.
